page: Amazon Web Services i3.xlarge is a storage-optimized virtual machine provisioned on the Xen hypervisor. It is powered by a 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor built on the x86_64 architecture, providing 4 virtual CPUs derived from 2 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. Memory capacity is allocated at 30.0 GB, which equates to 7.62 GB per physical core. A key characteristic of the instance is its local storage configuration, featuring a bundled 950 GB NVMe solid-state drive. Networking operates with a 1 Gbps baseline throughput, and the hardware environment does not include a GPU.

Benchmark evaluations reflect the older Broadwell-generation microarchitecture, placing raw CPU and memory metrics in lower tiers across standard synthetic suites. In stress-ng, the instance recorded a single-core score of 883.17 and a multi-core score of 2080.35, both ranking in the bottom 10%. Geekbench testing yielded 898.0 in single-core and 1900.0 in multi-core metrics. PassMark recorded an aggregate CPU score of 4511.88 and a memory score of 1713.72. Uncached large-block memory bandwidth reached 22.62 GB/sec for reads and 14.23 GB/sec for writes. In application benchmarks, the server achieved 2.54 million operations per second in Redis SET workloads and 2.81 GB/sec of static web serving throughput.

From an architectural standpoint, the trade-off in the i3.xlarge centers on local storage density versus compute processing power. While the CPU capability is constrained by legacy instruction sets and modest per-core throughput, the local NVMe drive delivers high direct-attached capacity without network storage protocol overhead. Resource balance favors IOPS-heavy operations over intensive mathematical computation or fast code compilation.

The Amazon Web Services i3.xlarge is suited for I/O-intensive workloads that require low-latency local disk access and moderate memory capacity. Target deployments include distributed NoSQL databases, transactional data stores, search indexing nodes, log analytics collectors, and caching layers with disk-backed persistence.
